| [NOTE-034](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-034.md) v2 | Curry et al. 2019, morality-as-cooperation in 60 societies | Coding 3,460 eHRAF paragraphs on the 60 Probability Sample Files societies found 962 morally valenced mentions of seven cooperative behaviours, 961 of them positive. | [NOTE-093](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-093.md) v2 | Bruckner — Welfare Subjects and Autopoiesis | Bruckner proposes, by abduction and not deduction (§4), that being autopoietic is sufficient, not necessary, for being a welfare subject. An entity is autopoietic when it "sustains, maintains, and renews itself in a way that responds and adapts to its environmental conditions". On this view insentient plants and a hypothetical non-sentient self-maintaining car ("Tessler") are welfare subjects, while engines with governors, thermostats and heat-seeking missiles are not. He answers the charge of absurd obligations in two ways: welfare value may not generate agent-neutral reasons at all, and if it does, the reasons concerning non-conscious subjects are "extremely weak" (Bradford 2023). | Read |
| [NOTE-097](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-097.md) v2 | Health and disease beyond social justice | Kukla's "institutional definition" makes a condition a health condition iff medicalising it would be best for collective wellbeing. Veit argues that any purely normativist definition of this kind defeats itself for two reasons. First, leaving "social justice" undefined lets a majority with other values medicalise what Kukla wanted to protect. Second, unless the institution of medicine is fixed from outside, the medical toolkit co-evolves until "health would simply become justice" (p. 15). His remedy is pluralism: at least three separate accounts, with justice linked to health empirically, not conceptually. | Read |
| [NOTE-098](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-098.md) v2 | Leonelli — Philosophy of Open Science | Leonelli argues that mainstream, institutional Open Science treats openness as the unlimited, digital sharing of research objects, a transparency-first ordering running transparency → quality (reproducibility) → inclusion. This rests on an object-oriented, "resourcist" epistemology of science. Four implementation cases (GISAID COVID data, open-source software stigma, crop-data linkage, the reproducibility "crisis") show it can narrow epistemic diversity and entrench epistemic injustice, which lowers reliability. She proposes instead "openness as judicious connection", grounded in a process-oriented view of research as the cultivation of "active knowledge". Her Figure 2 inverts the ordering to start from inclusion, and sharing becomes "neither a necessary starting point nor a sufficient condition" for reliable OS (p. 8). | Read |

| [NOTE-145](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-145.md) v2 | Douglas — Inductive risk and values in science | Hempel's "inductive risk" (the chance of wrongly accepting or rejecting a hypothesis) arises at three internal stages of science: choosing a methodology such as a significance level, characterising data, and interpreting results. Wherever the non-epistemic consequences of error can be foreseen, weighing them requires non-epistemic values. Douglas shows this on dioxin cancer studies. Three pathologist panels (1978, 1980, 1990) scored the same Kociba rat-liver slides differently (e.g. 34/50, 33/47, 18/50 tumours at 100 ng/kg/day). Choosing between threshold and no-threshold readings of the same data has meant regulatory limits about 100× apart. Values enter only indirectly, through the consequences of error, never as evidence that a claim is true. | Read |
| [NOTE-151](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-151.md) v2 | Register — The Depth of the Body | Register argues that body parthood "for moral purposes" is bounded below by depth. Depth is the microphysical commitment of an object's real definition, and objects that are "too deep" (a water molecule, the parcel of matter now composing the heart, a particular cloud server) are not body parts, though they are parts in the ordinary sense. His two principles ("bodily interests/rights are high-level") say that events which are high-level neutral do not bear on bodily rights or interests. So a BCI user's implemented software can be a body part owned by the user while the third-party server that runs it is not. | Read |
| [NOTE-156](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-156.md) v2 | Towards ethical evolution: responsible AI autonomy | The paper proposes, without implementation, formalism or experiment, that an AI system which designs further AI systems should pass on one "immutable" principle. The principle is: do not directly harm humanity or violate fundamental human values; monitor and mitigate misuse of your outputs; and make every derivative inherit this principle (p. 12). The mechanisms are a genetic-algorithm analogy, with immutable and mutable "genes", constrained crossover and filtered mutation, together with "temporal cloning". The paper is inconsistent about its central notion. The principle is enforced once by a penalty F = Q − α·P (p. 9) and once by "unbreachable" hard constraints (p. 13). | [NOTE-166](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-166.md) v2 | Personal Identity and Ethics (SEP) | A survey, arguing no thesis of its own, of how three contested questions bear on ethics: which account of persistence is true (unique psychological continuity, Shoemaker and Parfit; or biological continuity and animalism, Olson and DeGrazia), whether identity or the psychological relations (continuity and/or connectedness) is what matters (Parfit's fission case), and whether metaphysics constrains ethics or the reverse. | [NOTE-181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-181.md) v2 | The Moral Status of Animals (SEP) | The entry reviews five proposed grounds of moral considerability (species membership, human-exceptional capacities, personhood, sentience and agency). Its conclusion is that attempts to establish human uniqueness by capacities are "not the most promising" (§1.2). It then separates *having* moral status from the *weight* of a claim ("showing up on a moral radar screen", §2.2). Weight depends on the value theory adopted for animal interests (hedonism, preference satisfaction, objective list; §2.1) and on the normative framework (rights, which are absolute but generate forward-looking duties when violated, or a multi-factor utilitarianism). | [NOTE-185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-185.md) | The moral psychology of obligation | Tomasello proposes that the human sense of obligation is "the internalized social/rational pressure from a joint or collective self-regulating agent 'we'… to do what 'we' expect me to" (§3). | [NOTE-186](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-186.md) | Ethics of Parasocial Relationships | Fan–celebrity parasocial relationships are personal relationships (the fan relates to the celebrity as a unique individual, with reasons for partiality), built from three structural asymmetries: attention, communication and epistemic. | [NOTE-188](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-188.md) | The Weirdness of the World | The book's thesis is that every viable theory of how consciousness fits into the cosmos, and of the cosmos's basic structure, is both "bizarre" (contrary to common sense) and "dubious" (not rationally compelling). So "something that seems almost too crazy to believe must be true" (p. 4), and credence should be spread across the bizarre options. Examples of those options are that the United States is conscious (if materialism is true), that we are sims or Boltzmann brains (a 0.1–1% credence), that space is transcendentally ideal, that almost every act causes almost every future event, and that there is no fact about snail consciousness. Its only positive empirical results are three self-experiments against solipsism (for example, 17 of 19 decisive chess games lost, p < .001). Everything else is informal argument. | Read |
